newsitem.title: USA: Rubin repeats U.S. support for strong dollar.
newsitem.headline: Rubin repeats U.S. support for strong dollar.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar on Thursday.

"We have said repeatedly that in our judgment a strong dollar is in the best interest of the United Sates. It results in lower inflation, results in lower interest rates and it thereby helps feed a higher growth rate," said Rubin in a speech to the Investment Company Institute.
The dollar has tumbled as much as 10 percent to four-month lows against the yen in recent sessions amid signs that staunch U.S. support for the greenback was wavering.

Rubin in recent public comments has insisted his dollar policy was unchanged, but also said he agreed with Japanese officials' concerns about the weakening yen and cited the growing U.S.-Japanese trade gap.
Rubin added that he expected the economy to continue on its recent sound growth path.

"We have had ... really remarkably good fundamentals for the last four-and-a-half years and in my view, at least, I think the most likely scenario going forward for as far as I am comfortable looking forward is a continuation of good economic fundamentals."
But Rubin cautioned against undue optimism on the economy, noting that underlying economic problems could lurk beneath the current favorable data.
Strong current growth with low inflation and a shrinking federal budget deficit are positive signs, but no guarantee that economic problems will not arise in the future, he said.

"When you have such good conditions, I think there is a real risk that those favorable conditions will mask fundamental and underlying problems and reduce the probability that we will deal with them," Rubin said.
Rubin stressed that he remains optimistic that White House and Congressional negotiators will agree on a plan to balance the federal budget, despite thorny taxation issues.

"If we all continue to work with each other in the same spirit that led to the balanced budget agreement then I think we can bring it to a scuccessful conclusion and I think that will be very good for the country. It seems to me at least that the most difficult part of this will be the tax piece," he said.
Rubin projected that the deficit will continue to decline to $75 billion or less in the current fiscal year.
"It is now our judgment that (the deficit) could easily be in the 75 billion (dollars) or lower area this year," Rubin said.

Turning to the current prolonged debate over updating the nation's antiquated laws on banking and financial services, Rubin said the Clinton Administration would spell out its official position shortly.
"I expect that we will be announcing in the reasonably near future our views with respect to modernizing financial services," he said.

Regarding trade, Rubin said he was not optimistic that Congress would renew the president's "fast-track" authority to negotiate trade deals. Fast-track gives Congress only an "up-or-down" vote on trade pacts with no scope for modifying them.
"We are working with Congress to accomplish this right now, but I will tell you, it is going to be very difficult and the odds clearly are not in our favor," Rubin said.
